newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Experts meet in Vienna to discuss landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: Experts meet in Vienna to discuss landmine ban.

text.p: Government experts from more than 100 countries convened in Vienna on Wednesday to try to hammer out a blueprint for negotiations on a total worldwide ban on landmines.

"The function of the meeting will be to discuss the content of a convention (on banning landmines) and prepare the future negotiations," Thomas Hajnoczi, head of disarmament at the Austrian foreign ministry, told reporters before the conference began. Austria favours an immediate total ban.

The three-day conference is part of the so-called "Ottawa process" begun last October at a 50-nation forum hosted by Canada. The Canadian government aims for a legally-binding agreement in December 1997 to ban the production, stockpiling, export, and use of landmines.
Major mine producers such as the United States, Russia, Britain and France are among the delegates. China declined to attend.
Over 100 million landmines lie buried in 64 countries around the world. According to U.N. statistics landmines kill or maim a person every 20 minutes, or 25,000 people a year.
The issue of banning mines has gained a high profile recently, with Britain's Princess Diana taking up the cause after a trip to war-ravaged Angola last month.
United Nations Deputy Secretary-General Vladimir Petrovsky, attending the Vienna forum, said he was optimistic the conference would pave the way for an eventual solution.

"Multilateral negotiations always speed up the process, which is particularly important because the issue is so serious and we need to come from statements to practical actions," he told reporters outside the conference.

A separate initiative is under way at the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva of 61 members including China and Russia -- two top mine producers and exporters -- which have not taken part in the Ottawa talks.
Many governments prefer the issue to be negotiated by the Geneva body, which will meet three times this year, as they regard Canada's deadline as unrealistic.

But Donald Sinclair from the Canadian delegation pointed out that while the U.N. effort could complement the "Ottawa Process", no decision had yet been taken in Geneva to discuss the issue of landmines.

"The Conference on Disarmament has a legitimate role to play in this issue, should it decide to do so. At present anti-personnel mines are not on its agenda and no mandate has been agreed so as far as we are concerned there is only one process," he said.
The U.N.'s Petrovsky said he thought governments would opt to hold the final negotiations under the aegis of the U.N.
"There is a strong movement to have the negotiations in Geneva which does not exclude the negotiations in Ottawa. It could be a two-track approach," he said.
He did not believe the fact that China and Russia were not participating in the talks would prevent an agreement from being reached.

"In the course of negotiations I think there is always a possibility of accommodating the positions of countries," he said, citing the 1996 nuclear test ban treaty as an example of successful multilateral cooperation.
A follow-up conference to the Vienna forum is planned in Brussels in June before a December meeting in Ottawa.
